title: Effect Sovereignty
description_html:
This paper extends the constitutional syscall framework by arguing that all reality-touching operations should be expressed as governed system calls. Traditional architectures treat many external effects - GUI rendering, networking, storage persistence, time queries, sensor interaction - as library conveniences layered atop opaque runtime behavior. This diffusion obscures jurisdiction, hides authority assumptions, and undermines auditability.

We introduce the principle of effect sovereignty: any operation whose impact escapes the computational core must traverse an explicit constitutional boundary. System calls are generalized as the universal interface for world interaction, mediated by a typed admissibility function producing structured outcomes: execute, simulate, defer, or refuse.

The paper formalizes a minimal effect-boundary model, presents a taxonomy of reality-touching operations, and defines composable multi-authority adjudication chains spanning replay engines, runtimes, kernels, and hardware interfaces. A constitutional log structure enables deterministic replay and auditable refusal, replacing undefined behavior at the world boundary with structured accountability.

Rather than expanding the kernel surface, this model clarifies execution architecture: the computational core remains effect-pure, and all external interaction becomes explicitly governed. System calls evolve from privileged traps into constitutional acts mediating contact with reality.

This work complements the Substrate Migration Principle by illustrating how authority evaluation for world-touching effects can descend into enforceable substrate invariants.
